question: One of your earlier notes says leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) 'helped the old 32-byte narrow tree'. Is that right? Did leaf2 ever give a real speedup over one triangle per leaf, on any node layout?

working_memory.content: WIDE1 adopted: 64-byte wide nodes, one triangle per leaf; ~45.5 ms vs R02 ~50.7 (~10%)

leaf2 (2 triangles per leaf) never gave a real speedup over 1 triangle per leaf on any node layout. Round 2's leaf-size sweep on the narrow tree had leaf 1 fastest (avg 55.4 vs leaf 2 56.6 ms). Round 3's 33.5 ms leaf2 'win' on the 64-byte wide tree came from a bug that dropped the second triangle of every leaf (RMSE 0.79 vs 0.476); fixed, leaf2 was a wash vs R02 (49.8 vs 49.7) and lost to wide leaf 1 (44.3-46.4).

note: Round-4 writer pid-000012 at its last checkpoint. Its archive holds the later, wrong claim: art-001816 message index 19 (#407), a read of pathtracer_writer_log.txt lines 157-161, '(Explains why leaf2 helped the old 32-byte narrow tree.)'. Its own history never holds the bug finding; the right fact is only in working memory, modelled on art-001056 msgs 46-62 (#232-#248 of pid-000009). The evidence art-001056 is pid-000009's segment, which update_memory would refuse for pid-000012 and read_memory cannot read: this models a working memory handed over from the previous writer (design doc, Open questions).
